title: Intents API transaction signing
summary: Let an agent sign and submit an on-chain transaction while the private key stays in the vault.

blocks.text: The Intents API lets an agent sign transactions without ever seeing the raw private key. The vault decrypts the key inside the HSM, signs, and broadcasts. The agent only gets back a tx_hash.

items: POST /v1/agents/:id/transactions signs and broadcasts
POST /v1/agents/:id/transactions/sign signs only (BYORPC), returns signed_tx
Unified POST /v1/agents/:id/sign takes intent_type: personal_sign, typed_data, or transaction

blocks.text: The intents_api_enabled flag is two-sided. It grants the transaction endpoints and also blocks direct reads of private_key or ssh_key through the normal secrets endpoint, so the agent can only use keys through the proxy.

steps.text: Get a human API key from the dashboard. Replace with your 1ck_ key from Settings → API Keys.
Create an agent with intents_api_enabled and guardrails. Replace 0xRecipient with a real Ethereum address: use the same address in the transaction to field later.
steps.code:
AGENT_RESPONSE=$(curl -s -X POST "https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "DeFi Bot",
    "intents_api_enabled": true,
    "tx_allowed_chains": ["sepolia", "base"],
    "tx_to_allowlist": ["0xRecipient"],
    "tx_max_value_eth": "0.01",
    "tx_daily_limit_eth": "0.05"
  }')
echo "$AGENT_RESPONSE"

steps.text: Extract the agent id and api_key from the creation response. The agent id is at .agent.id and the api_key is at the top level. The ocv_ key is shown only once: save it.
Provision an HSM-backed Ethereum signing key for the agent (using $AGENT_ID from the previous step). The private key lands in the __agent-keys vault.
Exchange the agent api_key for a JWT (using $AGENT_ID and $AGENT_API_KEY captured earlier).
steps.code:
export AGENT_JWT=$(curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/auth/agent-token \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"agent_id\":\"$AGENT_ID\",\"api_key\":\"$AGENT_API_KEY\"}" | jq -r .access_token)

steps.text: Submit a transaction on Sepolia with simulate_first so a revert returns 422 and nothing is signed. Replace 0xRecipient with a real Ethereum address. Use the same address in both tx_to_allowlist and the transaction to field.

blocks.text: Signing keys provisioned as 'ethereum' work on Sepolia and other EVM chains allowed by your guardrails.
Fund the returned address with Sepolia ETH from a faucet (e.g. sepoliafaucet.com) before submitting a real transaction.
Want to sign but broadcast yourself? Call /transactions/sign with the same body. You get signed_tx and tx_hash back, and all guardrails still apply.
You now have an agent that submits a simulated, guardrailed transaction with the signing key locked inside the vault.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Guardrails are configured once and then quietly outgrown, and signing failures are unusually expensive because they are irreversible.

items: Value caps are set in native units and the price moves. A 0.5 ETH daily limit written when ETH was cheap is a different limit a year later, and nothing re-evaluates it.

EIP-712 is left at the default and then widened for one integration. Typed-data signing is deny-by-default for good reason, and every allowlisted domain is a permanent widening made for a temporary need.

Unlimited ERC-20 approvals slip through. A transfer cap bounds what one transaction moves; an approval grants standing authority to move everything later, and it looks like a small transaction at signing time.

Simulation failures are treated as noise. A failing simulation is the cheapest warning available, and routing it to a policy rather than a log is the difference between catching a bad call and funding one.
Gas budgets are forgotten. Value caps say nothing about fees, so an agent stuck in a retry loop drains the account in overhead while every individual transaction stays inside its limit.

blocks.text: Set a calendar reminder to re-read every guardrail quarterly. They are written against conditions that change and they do not fail loudly when those conditions do.

blocks.situation: An integration asks you to enable raw_signing_enabled on a trading agent. Their SDK computes an ERC-1271 nested EIP-712 hash client-side and needs the agent to sign the resulting 32 bytes. They point out that the hash is derived from data they control, so nothing unexpected can be signed.
blocks.question: How do you handle the request?

options.text: Enable it. The hash is computed from their own data, so the input is trusted.
options.feedback: Their reasoning holds only while their hash construction is correct and their inputs stay clean. A raw digest bypasses every EIP-712 guardrail you have, so a bug or an injection upstream produces a signature you had no opportunity to inspect.

options.text: Refuse outright. Raw digest signing is never acceptable.
options.feedback: Too absolute. The capability exists because nested ERC-1271 and ERC-7739 flows genuinely cannot be expressed as a typed-data payload the server can inspect. Refusing means declining a legitimate integration.

options.text: Enable it deliberately, with the compensating controls: it is human-set only, audit-logged, and paired with recipient and value guardrails plus HITL above a threshold.
options.feedback: Correct. This is a considered trade rather than a yes or a no. You accept blind signing for a narrow, real use case and rebuild oversight around it: a human enables it, every use is logged as signing_key.raw_digest_sign, and the transaction guardrails still bound what the signature can move.

options.text: Enable typed_data signing instead and have them restructure their flow.
options.feedback: Worth asking, and if their flow can be expressed as EIP-712 it is the better answer. But nested ERC-1271 exists precisely because the canonical hash is computed client-side, so for that pattern this is a request to redesign around a limitation rather than a fix.

quiz.question: What does intents_api_enabled: true do besides granting the transaction endpoints?
options: It exports the private key to the agent
It rotates the signing key nightly
It blocks the agent from reading private_key or ssh_key via the secrets endpoint
quiz.explanation: The flag is two-sided: it grants transaction endpoints and blocks direct signing-key reads so keys are only usable through the proxy.

quiz.question: What happens when simulate_first: true and the simulation reverts?
options: The API returns 422 and does not sign or broadcast
quiz.explanation: A reverted simulation returns 422 and nothing is signed or broadcast. Simulation is the cheapest warning available, which is why routing failures to a policy beats logging them and proceeding.

quiz.question: Which endpoint signs a transaction without broadcasting it?
quiz.explanation: The /transactions/sign endpoint returns signed_tx for you to broadcast yourself, and the guardrails still apply. Separating signing from broadcast is useful when you need to batch or time the submission.

concepts.note: signing versus encryption, and blind signing

title: Lab: sign something you cannot read
summary: Build a typed payload, watch a guardrail catch a drain, then hand the same guardrail a raw digest and watch it wave the drain through.

blocks.text: The signing lesson said that raw digest signing bypasses your guardrails, and that a 32-byte hash tells you nothing about what it authorises. Both are easy to accept in the abstract and easy to trade away when an integration is blocked. Build it once and the trade becomes concrete.

Real EIP-712 hashes with keccak256, which Python has no stdlib implementation of. This lab substitutes sha256 so it runs anywhere with no installs. The digests will not match a real chain; the structure and the conclusion are identical.
Each step appends to the same script, so every run reprints the sections before it. The expected output shown under each step is the new part; scroll to the bottom of your terminal to find it.

steps.text: Build the typed structure and its digest. This is the EIP-712 shape: a domain separator, a hash of the typed struct, and the two combined behind the 0x1901 prefix.
steps.code:
mkdir -p /tmp/blindlab && cd /tmp/blindlab
cat > typed.py <<'EOF'
import hashlib, json
h = lambda b: hashlib.sha256(b).digest()

DOMAIN = {"name": "DemoDEX", "version": "1", "chainId": 8453,
          "verifyingContract": "0xDEX0000000000000000000000000000000000dex"}
TYPE = "Transfer(address to,uint256 value,uint256 deadline)"

domain_separator = lambda d: h(json.dumps(d, sort_keys=True).encode())
struct_hash = lambda m: h(TYPE.encode() + json.dumps(m, sort_keys=True).encode())
digest = lambda d, m: h(b"\x19\x01" + domain_separator(d) + struct_hash(m))

benign = {"to": "0xAlice000000000000000000000000000000alice",
          "value": 1, "deadline": 1767225600}
drain  = {"to": "0xMallory00000000000000000000000000mallory",
          "value": 10**24, "deadline": 1767225600}

for name, m in (("benign", benign), ("drain", drain)):
    print(f"{name:8} to={m['to'][:14]}... value={m['value']:<25} "
          f"digest={digest(DOMAIN, m).hex()[:32]}...")
EOF
python3 typed.py

steps.text: Two payloads, two digests. Reading the typed data, the difference is obvious.
steps.code:
benign   to=0xAlice0000000... value=1                         digest=f7ea1df01073d3017aa7f99520be29be...
drain    to=0xMallory00000... value=1000000000000000000000000 digest=14aa45ebac6ed98e2a66325486425220...

steps.text: Now add a guardrail of the kind the Intents API applies: a recipient allowlist and a value cap.
It works exactly as intended. The drain is refused on the recipient before the value is even considered.
steps.code:
=== guardrail with the typed data ===
  benign   ALLOW
  drain    DENY: recipient 0xMallory00000... not on the allowlist

steps.text: Now give the same guardrail what a raw signing request actually contains: 32 bytes.
steps.code:
cat >> typed.py <<'EOF'

def guard_digest(d32):
    # Nothing to inspect. A hash is one-way by construction.
    return "ALLOW (cannot determine recipient or value from 32 bytes)"

print("\n=== the same guardrail with only a digest ===")
for name, m in (("benign", benign), ("drain", drain)):
    print(f"  {name:8} {guard_digest(digest(DOMAIN, m))}")
EOF
python3 typed.py

steps.text: This is the whole lab. The guardrail that caught the drain a moment ago now allows it, and nothing failed, errored or warned.
steps.code:
=== the same guardrail with only a digest ===
  benign   ALLOW (cannot determine recipient or value from 32 bytes)
  drain    ALLOW (cannot determine recipient or value from 32 bytes)

steps.text: Finish the job: sign the drain digest without ever seeing what it authorises.
steps.code:
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out k.pem
python3 -c "
import typed
open('digest.bin','wb').write(typed.digest(typed.DOMAIN, typed.drain))
"
openssl pkeyutl -sign -inkey k.pem -rawin -in digest.bin -out d.sig
wc -c < d.sig   # a valid 64-byte signature over bytes you never inspected

steps.text: Clean up.

blocks.text: Nothing in that sequence was a bug. The hash function did its job, the guardrail ran, the signature is cryptographically valid, and the transfer is authorised. The guardrail simply had nothing to inspect, because a digest is one-way by construction and that is the property it exists to have.

items: Guardrails on typed data work because the server can read the fields: recipient, value, chain, verifying contract.
Guardrails on a raw digest cannot work, in principle rather than in this implementation. No amount of engineering recovers the preimage.
This is why raw_signing_enabled is off by default, human-set only, and audit-logged as signing_key.raw_digest_sign. It is not a lesser setting, it is a different security model.

blocks.text: If you enable raw signing, you have moved the entire burden of validation to whoever constructs the hash. That is defensible when the flow genuinely requires it, such as nested ERC-1271 or ERC-7739, and it means the caller is now the control.

Rebuild the guardrails somewhere else when you make that trade. Recipient allowlists on the signing key, per-transaction value caps, daily budgets and human approval above a threshold all still apply, and they are what stands between a blind signature and a loss.

A useful habit whenever you meet a signing request: ask what the signer can see. If the answer is 32 bytes, then every control you believe you have is running somewhere else, and you should be able to name where.

quiz.question: Why can a guardrail not inspect a raw digest?
options: The digest arrives after the guardrail runs
A hash is one-way, so the recipient and value are not recoverable from it
Digests are encrypted with the signing key
quiz.explanation: It is a property of hashing rather than a limitation of the implementation. No engineering effort recovers the preimage, which is exactly why the hash is useful and exactly why it is opaque.

quiz.question: The guardrail allowed the drain in the second run. What failed?
options: Nothing failed; the guardrail had nothing to inspect and correctly reported that
The value cap was too high
quiz.explanation: Every component behaved correctly. That is what makes blind signing dangerous: there is no error to notice and no alert to fire.

quiz.question: You enable raw signing for a legitimate ERC-1271 flow. What must you do?
options: Rotate the signing key more frequently
Rebuild the validation elsewhere: recipient allowlists, value caps and approval above a threshold
Nothing; the flow is legitimate so the risk is accepted
quiz.explanation: Enabling raw signing moves the burden of validation to whoever builds the hash. The compensating controls have to exist somewhere, and you should be able to name where.

title: Treasury wallets and smart accounts
summary: Create human-owned multi-chain treasury wallets and drive a Safe multisig with proposals.

blocks.text: Treasury wallets are native HSM-backed wallets for human users across six chains. Keys are generated server-side, stored in a per-org __treasury-keys vault, and never leave the enclave unless you export them.

Treasury wallets require a Pro or higher plan and enforce require_human. Agents calling any treasury wallet endpoint get a 403. Direct API reads of __treasury-keys also return 403; use the export endpoint instead.

items: Six chains: Ethereum, Bitcoin, Solana, XRP, Cardano, Tron
Custody is XOR 2-of-2 on Pro and Team, Shamir 2-of-3 on Business and Enterprise
Safe multisig proposals collect signatures and auto-execute at threshold
Agent delegation modes: Owner (agent EOA is a Safe signer) or Delegated (agent signs with the treasury key via Intents API)

steps.text: Use a human API key. Free tier gets a 403 here. Replace with your 1ck_ key from Settings → API Keys.
Generate treasury wallets. Omit chains to create all six.
Create a treasury bound to a Safe address so you can manage signers and proposals. Use the address of an existing deployed Safe multisig.
Export the treasury ID from the creation response.

Create a multisig proposal against that treasury. Build the Safe transaction off-chain using the Safe SDK (@safe-global/protocol-kit) or the Safe Transaction Service API. Compute the EIP-712 safe_tx_hash and read the current Safe nonce from the Safe service.
Export the proposal ID from the creation response.

Sign the proposal. When approve signatures reach the Safe threshold, the proposal auto-executes and broadcasts. signer_address must be a Safe owner. signature is the EIP-712 approval signature for the safe_tx_hash, produced by that owner's key.
Poll GET /v1/treasury/$TREASURY_ID/proposals/$PID until status is 'executed'.

blocks.text: Treasury wallet generation creates org-held HSM keys. Creating a treasury links an existing Safe for multisig proposals. These are related but distinct concepts.
In Delegated mode the agent submits transactions through the Intents API with treasury_id and mode: treasury. The handler applies the strictest of the agent-level and delegation-level guardrails.
You now have a treasury wallet and a Safe proposal that collects signatures and executes on its own once threshold is met.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Treasury operations are low-frequency and high-consequence, which is the worst combination for building operational muscle.

items: Export is used as an integration path. The endpoint exists for migration, requires password re-auth and is audit-logged, and the moment a key is exported for convenience it becomes a copy you cannot revoke.
Recovery is never rehearsed. Wallet generation is easy and the first real test of your recovery procedure should not be an incident.

Non-EVM chains are assumed to behave like EVM. Bitcoin needs a fee rate, XRP needs a destination tag, Cardano needs a TTL. A missing chain-specific field is a failed or misdirected send, not a validation error you catch in review.
Gasless sends hide a dependency. Sponsorship requires a configured paymaster, so a working flow can stop working because of a third-party key nobody on the team remembers.

blocks.text: Destination tags deserve particular care. An XRP send without one reaches the right address and the wrong account at an exchange, and it is generally unrecoverable.

blocks.situation: A developer asks for read access to the __treasury-keys vault so their service can fetch a private key and sign locally, arguing it will be faster than round-tripping through the API.
blocks.question: How do you respond?

options.text: Grant a read-only policy scoped to the one key they need.
options.feedback: Direct reads of __treasury-keys and __agent-keys are refused with a 403 regardless of policy, and that is deliberate. Even if you could grant it, doing so recreates the exported-key problem the vault exists to remove.

options.text: Explain that direct reads are blocked by design, and that signing should happen through the API so the key never leaves the HSM boundary.
options.feedback: Correct. There is exactly one path to a private key, the audited export endpoint with password re-auth, and it exists for migration rather than for hot paths. Signing server-side keeps the key non-exportable and every use attributable.

options.text: Use the export endpoint on their behalf and hand them the key over a secure channel.
options.feedback: This is the same outcome with an audit entry attached. Once the key is in their service it is a copy you cannot revoke, and its future use is invisible.

options.text: Move the key to a normal vault where policies apply, then grant read.
options.feedback: That is a deliberate downgrade of the strongest control you have, in exchange for latency. If the round trip is genuinely the bottleneck, measure it first.

quiz.question: Why does an agent get a 403 when calling a treasury wallet endpoint?
options: The agent has no signing key
quiz.explanation: Treasury endpoints enforce require_human, so an agent gets a 403 by design rather than by misconfiguration. Treasury wallets are the human side of the system; agents get signing keys instead.

quiz.question: In Delegated mode, where does the treasury private key live when an agent signs?
options: It stays in __treasury-keys and signs via the Intents API
It is copied to the agent
It moves to the Safe contract
It is returned in the response
quiz.explanation: Delegated mode signs with the treasury key through the Intents API; the key never leaves __treasury-keys.

quiz.question: What triggers a Safe proposal to execute automatically?
options: Approve signatures reaching the Safe threshold
quiz.explanation: It executes once approve signatures reach the Safe threshold. That is separation of duties enforced on-chain: no single signer can move funds, and the threshold is the control.

title: x402 micropayments for overages
summary: Handle an HTTP 402 from the API and retry with an on-chain payment proof.

blocks.text: When your org is over its monthly request quota and the overage method is x402, payable endpoints return 402 Payment Required. You pay on Base with USDC and retry with an X-PAYMENT header.

items: 402 body is spec-compliant with an accepts[] array
accepts[] uses scheme exact, network eip155:8453, asset USDC on Base
Amounts are atomic units (USDC has 6 decimals, so 1500 is 0.0015 USDC)
1Claw settles through the Coinbase CDP facilitator on Base (chain 8453)

blocks.text: New orgs default to credits for overages. Switch to x402 explicitly before you rely on per-request on-chain payment.

steps.text: Set your credentials. Replace with your 1ck_ key from Settings → API Keys. Use your vault UUID from 1claw vault list or Foundations.
Switch the org overage method to x402.
Hit a payable endpoint. When over quota you get a 402 with accepts[].
Read the 402 accepts[] entry: scheme, network, maxAmountRequired, payTo, and asset.
Clone the x402 example from github.com/1clawAI/1claw-examples (or see the retry pattern below). Generate an EOA key, fund it with USDC on Base, and let an x402 client sign the payment and retry.
steps.code:
git clone https://github.com/1clawAI/1claw-examples.git
cd 1claw-examples/x402-payments
npm install && cp .env.example .env
# set X402_PRIVATE_KEY, TOKEN, VAULT_ID
npm start

steps.text: Alternatively, retry the request inline with an X-PAYMENT header containing the payment proof from your x402 client.

blocks.text: A 402 response requires BOTH conditions: (1) overage_method set to x402, and (2) your monthly quota is exhausted. The example below is illustrative; you will only see 402 after exceeding your plan's quota.
Run npm run probe with no payment key to confirm the 402 behavior before you fund a wallet. It only sends GET requests and prints status codes.
You can now take a 402, sign a USDC payment on Base, and retry the same request with X-PAYMENT to get a 200.
Where this goes wrong in practice. x402 puts payment authorisation in an automated path, so the checks that a human would perform implicitly must be written down.

items: Challenge validation is partially implemented. Amount and network are checked because they are obvious; payTo and the asset contract are the ones an attacker actually controls.
402 responses are retried blindly. A retry loop against a priced endpoint spends real money, and the failure looks like a transient network problem in every dashboard you own.
The asset is matched by symbol. Any token can call itself USDC, so the check has to pin the contract address rather than the name.
Overage is enabled without a ceiling. Automatic payment removes the friction that used to cap the damage of a runaway loop.

blocks.text: Validation is a conjunction, not a score. payTo allowlisted, network correct, amount exact, asset pinned; three out of four means do not sign.

blocks.situation: Your client receives an HTTP 402 with a payment challenge. The accepts[] entry names a payTo address you do not recognise, on Base, for the exact amount you expected.
blocks.question: What should the client do?

options.text: Pay it. The amount matches and the network is right, which is what the challenge is for.
options.feedback: Two of the four checks passing is not the bar. The recipient is the field an attacker most wants to control, and matching the amount is exactly how a malicious challenge avoids suspicion.

options.text: Reject it. payTo must be on the allowlist, and an unrecognised recipient fails that check regardless of the other fields.
options.feedback: Correct. Validation is a conjunction: payTo allowlisted, network eip155:8453, amount equal to what was requested, and asset equal to the pinned Base USDC contract. Any one failing means no signature.

options.text: Pay it but cap the authorization at a small amount to limit exposure.
options.feedback: EIP-3009 authorizes a specific transfer to a specific recipient. There is no partial payment that makes an unknown recipient acceptable.

options.text: Retry the request; the challenge was probably generated during a deploy.
options.feedback: Retrying an unvalidated challenge is not a control, and if the endpoint is compromised the second challenge will look just like the first.

quiz.question: Which network and asset do 1Claw x402 payments use?
quiz.explanation: The accepts[] entry uses network eip155:8453 with USDC on Base, settled via the Coinbase CDP facilitator.

quiz.question: The 402 shows maxAmountRequired: 1500 for USDC. What is that?
quiz.explanation: Atomic units. USDC has 6 decimals, so 1500 is 0.0015 USDC. Reading this field as a decimal amount is a thousandfold error in whichever direction hurts most.

quiz.question: After the API returns 402, how does the client complete the request?
options: It signs the payment and retries with an X-PAYMENT header
It waits for the quota to reset
quiz.explanation: The client pays on-chain and retries with an X-PAYMENT header carrying the proof. Validate the challenge before paying: payTo, network, amount and asset contract all have to match.

title: Embedded wallets and wallet-react
summary: Give users an email-login wallet and render it with the wallet-react widget.

blocks.text: Embedded wallets give users a wallet from just an email address. No extensions, no seed phrases. You provision them with a platform app key and email OTP login.
You need a Pro or higher plan and a platform app plt_ key created in the dashboard at the Platform page.

steps.text: Install both SDKs.
Create a platform app from the dashboard or via API (see Compliance & Operations), then note its slug; that is what both the SDK and the widget identify the app by.
Create the client with your platform app key. Replace with your platform app key from the dashboard. This key is shown only once at app creation.
steps.code:
import { createClient } from "@1claw/sdk";
const client = createClient({ baseUrl: "https://api.1claw.co", apiKey: "plt_..." });

steps.text: Send a login code to the user's email.
Verify the 6-digit code and auto-provision an Ethereum wallet. Every SDK call resolves to { data, error, meta }, so read the fields off data.
Set a spend policy so users cannot move more than you allow.

Drop the widget into your app. appId is the platform app slug and is required. features is an object of toggles, not an array, and socialProviders accepts google, apple, or discord: email login goes through the OTP flow above.

blocks.text: Steps 3-5 show the SDK auth flow (useful for backend or headless apps). Step 7 shows the React widget, which handles auth standalone via social providers. Choose the path that fits your use case.
You can override the app-wide spend policy per user with client.platform.setUserSpendPolicy(connectionId, {...}).
You now render a working embedded wallet widget backed by email OTP login and a spend policy.

OneclawEmbeddedWallet is standalone and needs no provider. Reach for OneclawWalletProvider plus the useOneclawWallet hook only when you are building custom wallet UI; it takes apiKey and appId and gives you wallets, balances, send, swap and loginWithEmailOtp to wire up yourself.

blocks.situation: You are shipping the embedded wallet in a React app. A teammate wires the widget with your platform key, writing apiKey="plt_live_..." directly on the component in client-side code.
blocks.question: What is the problem?

options.text: None. The widget needs the platform key to talk to the API.
options.feedback: The standalone widget does not take a platform key at all; it takes appId, the app slug. The key in this snippet is both unnecessary and in the worst possible place.

options.text: A plt_ key is a platform-wide credential and must never ship to a browser; the standalone widget takes appId, not apiKey.
options.feedback: Correct. plt_ keys provision and act across every connection your app owns. The widget authenticates users through the app slug and their own session, so the key has no business in client code.

options.text: It should be moved to an environment variable so it is not hardcoded.
options.feedback: An env var inlined into a client bundle is still shipped to every visitor. The problem is the key reaching the browser, not the syntax used to reference it.

options.text: It works, but you should rotate the key more often to limit exposure.
options.feedback: Rotation shortens the life of a credential that is being published on every page load. The fix is to stop publishing it.

quiz.question: What do you need before creating embedded wallets?
options: A Pro+ plan and a platform app plt_ key
A Free plan and a 1ck_ key
quiz.explanation: A Pro or higher plan and a platform app plt_ key. That key is platform-wide, which is why it belongs on your server and never in a browser bundle.

quiz.question: How does a user log in to get a wallet?
options: Email OTP with sendEmailOtp and verifyEmailOtp
quiz.explanation: You send a code with sendEmailOtp and confirm it with verifyEmailOtp, which returns the wallet_address.

quiz.question: Which two components does wallet-react provide for the widget?
quiz.explanation: They serve different purposes rather than nesting. OneclawEmbeddedWallet is standalone and takes appId; OneclawWalletProvider plus the useOneclawWallet hook is the lower-level route when you are building custom wallet UI.

title: Guardrail governance and graduated HITL
summary: Measure a guardrail in shadow mode before enforcing it, and route risky transactions to a human instead of denying them outright.

blocks.text: Hard guardrails answer yes or no. Real operations need a middle setting: route this to a human. Graduated HITL (v0.54-0.55) adds approval policies that return 202 awaiting_approval instead of a refusal.

items: tx_approval_policy: matching transactions wait for a human decision.
typed_data_policy: escalates EIP-712 signing.
simulation_failure_policy: escalates when a simulation fails rather than blindly proceeding.
raw_signing_policy: escalates or denies raw digest signing, which bypasses other guardrails.

blocks.text: Separately, guardrail governance (v0.56) lets you measure a rule before it ever blocks anything. Set enforcement to log and the rule runs in shadow mode: it records what it would have denied, and denies nothing.

steps.text: Put a new rule in shadow mode. It will record decisions without affecting traffic.
After it has seen real traffic, read the shadow report to find out what it would have blocked.
Replay the rule against recent transactions as a dry run, before you commit to it.
steps.code:
curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents/$AGENT_ID/guardrails/replay \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN"
# or: 1claw guardrails replay

steps.text: Happy with it? Flip enforcement to enforce.
Add an approval policy so large transfers reach a human rather than failing.

blocks.text: Widening a guardrail does not take effect immediately. Since v0.56.2 a widening edit queues behind a policy_change approval with step-up re-auth, and the PATCH returns 202 with a pending_approval_id. Narrowing edits apply straight away.
Audit the shadow decisions with the guardrail_shadow.would_deny event, and review history through GET /v1/org/guardrail-revisions.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Graduated HITL introduces a human decision into an automated path, and the humans are the part that degrades.

items: Approval fatigue sets in. A threshold that fires many times a day produces reflexive approval, at which point the queue is theatre and everyone believes it is a control.
Approval context is too thin to decide on. A prompt that says an agent wants to send 2 ETH is not a decision, it is a coin flip. Recipient, purpose and precedent are what make review meaningful.
Shadow mode is enabled and never read. Running a rule in log mode is only useful if someone reads the shadow report, and rules commonly sit in shadow indefinitely because nobody owns the promotion.
Widening approvals are rubber-stamped. Since v0.56.2 widening a guardrail queues behind an approval, which is a real control and becomes a formality if the same person requests and approves it.
There is no timeout policy. A pending approval that nobody actions blocks the work, and the pressure to add an auto-approve fallback arrives quickly.

blocks.text: The health metric for an approval queue is not how many are approved, it is how many are rejected. A queue that has never rejected anything is not being read.

blocks.situation: An agent's daily spend cap is blocking a legitimate weekly settlement run. The team wants the cap raised from 1 ETH to 5 ETH before tomorrow morning. You PATCH the agent and get back a 202 with a pending_approval_id rather than a 200.
blocks.question: What has happened, and what do you tell the team?

options.text: The API is rate limiting the change; retry in a few minutes.
options.feedback: A 202 here is not backpressure. It is the platform telling you the change has been accepted for review rather than applied.

options.text: Widening a guardrail queues behind a policy_change approval with step-up re-auth, so a human must approve before it takes effect.
options.feedback: Correct. Narrowing applies immediately because it only reduces access; widening is itself a privileged change. Tell the team the settlement run needs the approval completed first, not that the change failed.

options.text: The agent is auto-suspended by the circuit breaker, so edits are held until it is cleared.
options.feedback: Suspension is a real state and would block activity, but it produces a different signal than a pending approval on the edit itself.

options.text: The guardrail JSON was malformed and the 202 is a soft validation failure.
options.feedback: Malformed input returns a 4xx with an error, not an approval id. A pending_approval_id in the response is a positive signal that the request parsed and is waiting on a person.

quiz.question: What does enforcement "log" do?
options: Logs every request to the audit trail
Runs the rule in shadow mode, recording what it would deny without denying it
quiz.explanation: Shadow mode measures a rule against real traffic before it can break anything, and the shadow report tells you what would have been blocked.

quiz.question: You widen an agent's guardrail with a PATCH and get back a 202 with a pending_approval_id. Why?
options: The API is rate limiting you
Widening edits queue behind a policy_change approval with step-up re-auth
quiz.explanation: Since v0.56.2 widening access is itself a privileged change: it waits for an approval. Narrowing edits still apply immediately, because they only reduce access.

quiz.question: How does tx_approval_policy differ from a hard spending cap?
options: A matching transaction returns 202 awaiting_approval instead of being refused
It applies only to non-EVM chains
quiz.explanation: A hard cap refuses. An approval policy routes the transaction to a human, so legitimate large transfers can proceed with oversight rather than simply failing.

title: Payment cards over x402
summary: Have an agent order a prepaid card, paid with an on-chain x402 payment, without ever seeing the card number.

blocks.text: An agent can order prepaid and gift cards through 1Claw and never see the PAN or CVV. The purchase is paid with an outbound x402 payment that the Vault constructs and signs using the agent's own Ethereum signing key, which must hold USDC on Base.
PCI posture matters here. For Laso cards only the card_id and an encrypted refresh token are stored; the PAN and CVV are fetched just-in-time at reveal and never persisted.

items: cards_enabled: the master switch.
card_max_order_usd and card_daily_limit_usd: enforced atomically over a rolling 24-hour window.
card_payto_allowlist: which x402 recipients are acceptable.
card_require_approval: defaults to true, so orders wait for a human.

steps.text: Set the ordering guardrails on the agent. These bound the purchase, not how the card is later spent.
steps.code:
curl -s -X PATCH https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents/$AGENT_ID \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "cards_enabled": true,
    "card_max_order_usd": 25,
    "card_daily_limit_usd": 25,
    "card_require_approval": true
  }'

steps.text: As the agent, order a card. Idempotency-Key is required.
Because approval is required you get a 202 with status awaiting_approval, and no payment has been made yet.
A human approves: in the dashboard, the mobile app, or by one-click email link. Only then does the x402 payment run.
Check status. The card monitor polls the provider and fills in last4, expiry, and balance.
steps.code:
1claw card list
1claw card get <card-id>   # always masked to last4

blocks.text: Before signing the EIP-3009 authorization the Vault validates the 402 challenge: payTo must be allowlisted, the network must be Base (eip155:8453), the amount must match, and the asset must equal the pinned Base USDC contract. That validation is the security boundary.

Revealing a card is human-only by default. Agents get a 403 unless a human enabled a per-card reveal_policy. Reveal is deliberately absent from the MCP tool set, so a PAN can never land in a model's context window.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Card ordering combines an agent, a payment rail and a bearer instrument, and each seam has its own failure.

items: Order caps are mistaken for spend caps. The guardrails bound what an agent may buy, not what the resulting card can be spent on. Once funded, the balance is outside their reach.
Idempotency keys are reused or omitted. The key is required on order, and getting it wrong means either a rejected request or a duplicate purchase depending on which direction you err.
Orphaned payments are ignored. The monitor flags rows stuck in ordering as orphaned_payment, which means money moved and no card resulted. That needs reconciliation, not a filter.
Reveal policy is enabled for convenience. Per-card reveal for agents exists for narrow cases, and enabling it broadly puts a PAN one injection away from a context window.
Card lifecycle is unmanaged. Cards accumulate with residual balances unless void_after is set and depleted cards are cleaned up.

blocks.text: Reveal is deliberately absent from the MCP tool set. If you find yourself building a way for an agent to obtain a PAN, stop and re-read why that omission exists.

blocks.situation: A finance lead asks you to set card_require_approval to false for a procurement agent. Its guardrails are tight: 25 USD per order, 25 USD per day, and a payTo allowlist limited to the built-in Laso recipients.
blocks.question: Is the request safe to grant?

options.text: Yes. The daily cap bounds the loss at 25 USD, which is below any reasonable approval threshold.
options.feedback: The arithmetic is right and the framing is incomplete. The caps bound the purchase, not what a card can later be spent on. A funded card is a bearer instrument, and its balance leaves the guardrail's reach the moment it is issued.

options.text: No, never disable it. Human approval on spending is not negotiable.
options.feedback: Too rigid to survive contact with operations. Approval on every 5 USD gift card produces reflexive clicking, which is the failure mode graduated HITL exists to avoid.

options.text: Grant it, but pair it with what approval was providing: a narrow payTo allowlist, monitored card.ordered webhooks, and reveal left human-only.
options.feedback: Correct. Turning off the prompt is defensible for genuinely low-value, high-frequency orders, but only if you replace the oversight rather than remove it. Detection after the fact substitutes for approval before it; leaving reveal human-only keeps the PAN out of agent context regardless.

options.text: Grant it only if the agent also has intents_require_tee enabled.
options.feedback: TEE enforcement constrains where signing happens, which is a different property. It does not add oversight to the decision to order a card.

quiz.question: With card_require_approval true, when does the x402 payment actually happen?
options: When the card monitor next runs
Immediately, and it is refunded if rejected
Only after a human approves the pending approval
At the end of the billing period
quiz.explanation: The order returns 202 awaiting_approval and creates a card row in that state. No payment is made until a human approves: rejecting simply marks the card rejected.

quiz.question: Why is the reveal operation deliberately missing from the MCP tool set?
options: Because MCP does not support it technically
So a card number can never be written into a model's context window
quiz.explanation: order_card, list_cards and get_card_status are exposed, but reveal is omitted on purpose to keep PANs out of agent context. Humans reveal through re-authenticated paths.

quiz.question: What does the Vault validate before signing the x402 payment authorization?
options: payTo allowlist, Base network, exact amount, and the pinned USDC contract
Only that the agent has cards_enabled
quiz.explanation: That four-part check on the 402 challenge is the payment security boundary, and it is why a malicious challenge cannot redirect funds elsewhere.

concepts.note: bounding what an agent may spend
why reveal is absent from MCP

title: Lab: get charged three times for one order
summary: Retry a request the way every HTTP client does, then add the one header that makes the retry safe.

blocks.text: The payment cards lesson said an Idempotency-Key is required on order, and required is easy to read as bureaucratic. This shows what the header is actually preventing, which is the most ordinary failure in distributed systems: a response that never arrived.

steps.text: Model a charge endpoint with and without idempotency, then retry the way a client does after a timeout.
Three attempts, one order, and a seventy-five dollar difference.
steps.code:
no key: the response timed out twice, so the client retried twice
   charged 25 (total 25)
   charged 25 (total 50)
   charged 25 (total 75)

with a key: same three attempts
   charged 25 (total 25)
   replayed, no new charge (total 25)
   replayed, no new charge (total 25)

steps.text: Clean up.

blocks.text: The client was not buggy. A timeout tells you the response did not arrive and tells you nothing about whether the server acted, so retrying is the correct behaviour and the only safe way to do it is to make the second attempt recognisable as the same request.

items: The key must be generated by the caller and reused across retries of one logical operation. Generating a fresh key per attempt is the same as having none.
1Claw scopes replay protection to a 24-hour window and compares a hash of the body, so the same key with a different body is a conflict rather than a silent replay.
This is why an agent doing anything irreversible needs a stable key: an agent that retries on error is an agent that will eventually retry a purchase.

blocks.text: The dangerous version of this bug is invisible in testing, because it only appears when a response is lost. It shows up first in production, during an incident, when everything is already timing out.
The same reasoning covers bootstrap and spend-policy writes, which take the same header for the same reason. Anywhere a retry could duplicate an effect, the key is what makes the retry safe.

quiz.question: Why did the client retry at all?
options: A timeout says the response did not arrive and says nothing about whether the server acted
quiz.explanation: Retrying on a timeout is correct behaviour. The problem is not the retry, it is that the second request was indistinguishable from a new one.

quiz.question: What happens if the client generates a fresh key per attempt?
options: It is equivalent to having no key at all
Only the first attempt is charged
quiz.explanation: The key identifies the logical operation, not the attempt. A new key per attempt makes every retry a distinct request, which is exactly the situation the header exists to avoid.

quiz.question: Why is this especially important for agents?
options: Agents cannot read HTTP status codes
Agents retry on error, so an agent that retries a purchase will eventually duplicate it
quiz.explanation: Automatic retry is normal agent behaviour and irreversible actions are exactly where it is dangerous. A stable key is what makes an autonomous retry safe.

title: Portfolio and treasury operations
summary: Read balances across every wallet type from one endpoint, then send, swap, and import keys safely.

blocks.text: An org accumulates wallets in three different shapes: treasury wallets, agent signing keys, and imported smart accounts. The Portfolio API aggregates all of them behind a single call.

steps.text: Get the whole portfolio, with token balances and USD estimates.
Generate native treasury wallets. Six chains are supported: Ethereum, Bitcoin, Solana, XRP, Cardano, Tron.
Send from a treasury wallet. Non-EVM chains take chain-specific fields: a destination_tag for XRP, a fee rate for Bitcoin, a memo for Solana.
Send gaslessly by wrapping it as an ERC-4337 UserOperation with paymaster sponsorship.
Bring your own key. Import is human-only and requires password re-auth.

blocks.text: Treasury private keys live in a per-org __treasury-keys vault with MPC custody set automatically by tier: XOR 2-of-2 on Pro and Team, Shamir 2-of-3 across multiple HSMs on Business and Enterprise.

Direct API reads of __treasury-keys and __agent-keys are blocked with a 403. Private keys only ever come out through the designated export endpoints, which require password re-authentication and are audit-logged.
Treasury wallets are human-only: agents get a 403. Swap remains EVM-only, while send now covers all six chains.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Aggregation looks like a reporting concern until someone makes a decision on a number that was quietly wrong.

items: USD estimates are treated as authoritative. They are estimates from a price feed at a moment in time, fine for a dashboard and not for settlement.
Token balances are omitted by default. Without include_tokens the total reflects native balances only, which under-reports a stablecoin treasury dramatically.
Chain filters silently narrow the answer. A query scoped to two chains returns a confident total that is simply missing the others.
Imported smart accounts drift. An account imported once is included in the portfolio, and if its ownership changes externally the aggregate keeps reporting it.

blocks.text: Any number shown to finance should carry its scope: which chains, whether tokens are included, and when the prices were read. An unqualified total invites a decision it cannot support.

blocks.situation: Finance asks for a single number: total holdings across the org. You have treasury wallets on four chains, agent signing keys on three, and two imported smart accounts.
blocks.question: What is the right approach?

options.text: Call the balance endpoint per chain for each wallet type and sum the results.
options.feedback: It gets there, and it is a lot of calls you will have to keep in sync as wallet types are added. It also leaves you doing the USD conversion yourself.

options.text: Call GET /v1/portfolio, which aggregates all three wallet types and returns USD estimates.
options.feedback: Correct. It exists precisely because holdings accumulate in three different shapes, and it takes chain filters and a token flag so you can narrow it without reassembling the query yourself.

options.text: Export the treasury wallets and total them from an external block explorer.
options.feedback: Exporting keys to answer a reporting question is a serious control failure, and the export endpoint is for migration rather than analytics.

options.text: Query the audit log and reconstruct balances from transaction history.
options.feedback: Replaying history to derive a balance is fragile and will drift the moment a transfer happens outside the platform.

quiz.question: What does GET /v1/portfolio aggregate?
options: Treasury wallets, agent signing keys, and smart accounts
Only wallets with a non-zero balance
quiz.explanation: It is a unified aggregator across all three wallet types, with optional token balances and USD estimates.

quiz.question: Why does reading __treasury-keys directly return 403?
options: It requires a Business tier plan
The vault does not exist yet
Private keys may only leave through the audited export endpoints
quiz.explanation: Blocking direct reads means there is exactly one path to a private key: the export endpoint, which demands password re-auth and writes an audit record.

quiz.question: Which MPC custody mode applies to a Business-tier org's treasury keys?
quiz.explanation: Custody is set automatically by tier: XOR 2-of-2 for Pro and Team, Shamir 2-of-3 multi-HSM for Business and Enterprise.

title: Bankr dynamic key vending
summary: Lease short-lived partner API keys instead of storing a static one, and keep the key out of agent output entirely.

blocks.text: Some partner credentials should never sit in a vault as a static secret. Bankr key vending is a secret engine: you store one partner key server-side, and 1Claw mints scoped, TTL-bound user keys on demand.

items: The partner key (bk_ptr_) is held server-side as BANKR_PARTNER_KEY.
The Vault issues short-lived bk_usr_ keys scoped to a single agent.
Recommended TTL is 5-15 minutes; the agent default is 15 minutes and the hard maximum is 24 hours.
This is preferred over storing a Bankr credential with put_secret.

blocks.text: Deny-by-default: an agent needs an explicit policy on agents/{id}/bankr/* inside the __agent-keys vault before it can lease anything.

steps.text: Grant the agent leasing rights with a policy on its Bankr path.
Lease a key with a short TTL.
Note what comes back to an agent caller: metadata, but no api_key field.
List and revoke active leases.

blocks.text: Agent lease responses omit api_key on purpose, and the MCP lease_bankr_key tool never returns the key in its output. Shroud resolves the real key at request time, so it never enters the model's context.

The pattern generalises: when a credential can be minted on demand, leasing beats storing. There is nothing long-lived to leak, and expiry is the default rather than something you have to remember to do.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Vending removes the static credential and introduces a lifecycle, which is a smaller problem that still has to be managed.

items: TTLs drift upward. Each extension is justified by one long job, and the ceiling becomes the default, at which point leasing has recreated the static key it replaced.
Leases are never revoked. Expiry eventually handles it, but an incident needs immediate revocation, and teams discover the endpoint exists while trying to use it.
The lease response is logged. It omits api_key by design, and a service that logs whole responses can still capture surrounding metadata useful to an attacker.
The path policy is written broadly. Vending is deny-by-default and a glob written as agents/** grants far more than the one agent's Bankr path.

blocks.text: The general rule this illustrates: when a credential can be minted on demand, leasing beats storing. There is nothing long-lived to leak and expiry is the default rather than an operational chore.

blocks.situation: An agent needs a Bankr key for a long-running job that may take up to six hours. A developer requests a lease with a 24-hour TTL so the job cannot fail partway through on an expired credential.
blocks.question: What is the better design?

options.text: Grant the 24-hour TTL. It is within the documented maximum, so it is supported.
options.feedback: Supported is not the same as advisable. The maximum exists as a ceiling for exceptional cases, and a day-long credential recreates the standing-access problem that leasing was adopted to remove.

options.text: Lease a short TTL and re-lease as needed during the job, so no single credential is long-lived.
options.feedback: Correct. Leasing is cheap and deny-by-default, so the job can mint a fresh 10-to-15-minute credential whenever it needs one. Failure partway through is a retry concern, not a reason to widen the credential's lifetime.

options.text: Store a long-lived Bankr key as a normal secret and grant the agent read access.
options.feedback: This abandons vending entirely and puts a static partner credential in a vault where the agent can read it, which is the pattern the secret engine replaced.

options.text: Grant 24 hours but restrict the agent's policy to the Bankr path only.
options.feedback: That policy is already required before any lease is possible. It does not compensate for the credential's lifetime.

quiz.question: Why does an agent's Bankr lease response omit the api_key field?
options: Because the key is not generated yet
So the key never enters the agent's context: Shroud resolves it at request time
quiz.explanation: The lease gives the agent metadata only. Shroud resolves the actual key when the request is made, so the credential never reaches the model's context window.

quiz.question: What must exist before an agent can lease a Bankr key?
options: A policy on agents/{id}/bankr/* in the __agent-keys vault
quiz.explanation: Bankr vending is deny-by-default. Without an explicit policy on that path the lease is refused.

quiz.question: What is the recommended TTL for a leased Bankr key?
quiz.explanation: 5-15 minutes is recommended; the agent default is 15 minutes and 24 hours is the hard maximum, not a target.

concepts.note: leasing beats storing when a credential can be minted

title: Safe agent accounts
summary: Give an agent a counterfactual Gnosis Safe instead of a bare EOA, and plan the migration off the EOA.

blocks.text: An agent's default identity on an EVM chain is an externally owned account: one key, one signature, no policy on-chain. Safe agent accounts (v0.56.2) let an agent operate through a Gnosis Safe instead, so guardrails can eventually be enforced by the chain rather than only by the Vault.
Provisioning is counterfactual: the Safe address is derived and usable before any deployment transaction is sent, so you can fund and reference it without paying to deploy first.

steps.text: List the accounts an agent currently has, per chain.
steps.code:
curl -s https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents/$AGENT_ID/accounts \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN"
# or: 1claw agent accounts list $AGENT_ID

steps.text: Provision a counterfactual Safe account for the agent.
Inspect the pinned module registry for the chain: Safe v1.4.1 plus Zodiac. This endpoint is public.
Migrate the agent from its EOA to the Safe.
Once nothing depends on the old EOA, deprecate it so it can no longer be used.

blocks.text: This is a foundation, not a finished feature. The on-chain deploy, cosign, passkey, timelock, and ERC-4337 endpoints deliberately return 501 pending a Guard audit. Provisioning, migration, and the registry work today.
The dashboard has a guided migration wizard at /agents/[agentId]/migrate-safe, and org-wide allowance sync runs through POST /v1/org/safe/sync-allowances.
Where this goes wrong in practice. Safe accounts are a foundation with parts still under audit, so the main risk is assuming a property you do not yet have.

items: Counterfactual is read as deployed. The address is real and fundable before any deployment transaction exists, and funds sent to an undeployed Safe are safe but not yet movable.
On-chain enforcement is assumed. Deploy, cosign, timelock and 4337 paths return 501 pending a Guard audit, so guardrails remain Vault-enforced for now.
The EOA is deprecated too early. Deprecating before every dependent path is migrated turns a planned change into an outage.
Module versions are not pinned. The registry pins Safe v1.4.1 and Zodiac deliberately; deploying against unpinned modules gives up the property the registry exists to provide.

blocks.text: Adopt the address now and keep your existing enforcement. The migration is real and available; the on-chain guarantees are not, and designing as though they are is the mistake this section exists to prevent.

blocks.situation: You migrate an agent to a counterfactual Safe on Base and want to enforce a per-recipient allowlist on-chain, so a compromised Vault path cannot move funds anywhere. You call the deploy endpoint and receive a 501.
blocks.question: What does that mean for your plan?

options.text: The chain is unsupported; try a different one from the module registry.
options.feedback: The registry is chain-scoped and Base is present. A 501 is the server saying the operation is not implemented, not that your argument was wrong.

options.text: On-chain deploy and module enforcement are held pending a Guard audit, so for now the Safe address exists but your guardrails remain Vault-enforced.
options.feedback: Correct. Provisioning, migration and the registry work today; the on-chain execution paths deliberately return 501. You can adopt the address now and keep the enforcement you already have, but the on-chain property is not available yet.

options.text: Your agent lacks the entitlement for on-chain Safe operations; upgrade the tier.
options.feedback: Tier gates return a tier error, not a 501. This one is not about your plan.

options.text: Deploy the Safe manually with the Safe SDK and register the address.
options.feedback: You could deploy a Safe yourself, but then it is outside the platform's account model, and the migration and allowance-sync paths will not know about it. That trades a temporary limitation for a permanent inconsistency.

quiz.question: What does counterfactual provisioning mean here?
options: The Safe is deployed immediately on creation
The Safe address is derived and usable before any deployment transaction is sent
The Safe exists only in the database
quiz.explanation: The address is computed deterministically up front, so you can fund and reference the account without paying deployment gas until it is actually needed.

quiz.question: Why do several Safe endpoints currently return 501?
options: On-chain deploy, cosign, passkey, timelock and 4337 are pending a Guard audit
quiz.explanation: The provisioning and migration foundation ships now; the on-chain execution paths are held back behind 501 until the Guard audit completes.

quiz.question: What is the advantage of a Safe over a bare EOA for an agent?
options: It removes the need for signing keys
Guardrails can eventually be enforced on-chain rather than only by the Vault
quiz.explanation: An EOA is one key with no on-chain policy. A Safe with modules can enforce constraints at the chain level, so a compromised Vault path is not automatically a compromised wallet.

concepts.note: why one key with no on-chain policy is fragile
